content: Exercise intolerance refers to a condition in which an individual is unable to perform physical exercise at a level that would typically be expected for their general physical condition. Alternatively, they may experience unusually severe symptoms following exercise, such as pain, fatigue, or other adverse effects. It is important to note that exercise intolerance is not a disease or syndrome in itself but rather a symptom indicative of an underlying issue. The term exercise intolerance can be somewhat ambiguous, as there are numerous potential reasons why physical activity might be limited. For example, a patient might experience symptoms such as excessive breathlessness (dyspnea), muscle pain (myalgia), or progressive muscle weakness during exercise. Alternatively, they may develop severe headaches, nausea, or extreme fatigue after exercising. Identifying the specific cause of exercise intolerance is often critical in diagnosing the underlying disease. Exercise intolerance is commonly associated with certain medical conditions, particularly organic brain diseases, mitochondrial disorders, and neuromuscular diseases. In some cases, it may be one of the only symptoms of a condition, such as in less severe forms of metabolic myopathies. Additionally, nonspecific fatigue or pain syndromes, including chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, and overtraining syndrome, often include exercise intolerance as a prominent symptom. Certain cardiac conditions, such as heart block or junctional bradycardia, can also lead to exercise intolerance. Other health issues, including cardiac arrhythmias (abnormal heart rate or rhythm) or aortic valve insufficiency, may cause significant activity limitations, such as shortness of breath or reduced exercise capacity. Similarly, individuals with degenerative spinal conditions may experience exercise limitations due to muscle spasms or restricted spinal motion. Exercise is often a critical component of treatment for patients with heart or back conditions, and tailored exercise regimens are available for these groups. Healthcare professionals, including physical therapists and athletic trainers, are trained to modify exercise programs to suit the specific needs of these patients. However, there are certain medical conditions where exercise, particularly in the context of rehabilitation, may be contraindicated. These include, but are not limited to: Decompensated heart failure Recent myocardial infarction (MI) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or cardiomyopathy following recent myocarditis Active or suspected myocarditis or pericarditis Low left ventricular ejection fraction Severe aortic stenosis Unstable ischemia Unstable arrhythmias Resting pulse greater than 100 beats per minute Resting systolic blood pressure >200 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure >110 mmHg Severe pulmonary hypertension Suspected or known dissecting aneurysm Recent systemic or pulmonary embolism Pneumothorax or hemoptysis Thrombophlebitis Other conditions may also preclude exercise under specific circumstances. In some cases, passive physiotherapy may serve as an alternative for patients who are unable to safely engage in self-powered physical activity.
